heat-treatment-001.question: Which statement about the martensitic transformation in steel is correct?
choices: It proceeds as carbon atoms diffuse over long distances and precipitate cementite at grain boundaries
It is a diffusionless shear transformation producing body-centered tetragonal (BCT) martensite supersaturated with carbon
The slower the cooling rate, the more time carbon has to diffuse, so the more martensite forms
heat-treatment-001.explanation: When austenite is quenched faster than the critical cooling rate, carbon has no time to diffuse, and a shear-type transformation occurs in which atoms shift cooperatively by small amounts, producing body-centered tetragonal (BCT) martensite supersaturated with carbon. Because the carbon distorts the lattice along the c axis, martensite is very hard and brittle. The transformation starts at the Ms temperature and progresses as the temperature falls, with almost no dependence on holding time. Pearlite and bainite are the structures that separate into ferrite and cementite with carbon diffusion, and it is pearlite that forms more readily the slower the cooling.

heat-treatment-002.question: Which correctly describes the difference between a TTT (isothermal transformation) diagram and a CCT (continuous cooling transformation) diagram?
choices: A TTT diagram shows transformation when the steel is quenched to a fixed temperature and held there, while a CCT diagram shows transformation during continuous cooling
A TTT diagram shows transformation during continuous cooling, while a CCT diagram shows transformation when the steel is held at a fixed temperature
The two contain the same information, with the vertical and horizontal axes swapped
heat-treatment-002.explanation: A TTT diagram shows the start and finish times of transformation when austenitized steel is quenched to a given temperature fast enough to avoid transformation and then held at that temperature; it is used to design isothermal treatments such as austempering. When the temperature falls continuously, as in actual quenching, the CCT diagram applies, and its transformation start line is shifted to longer times and lower temperatures than in the TTT diagram. The choice assigning continuous cooling to the TTT diagram and isothermal holding to the CCT diagram swaps the two definitions. Both are separate diagrams with temperature on the vertical axis and time (logarithmic) on the horizontal axis, and cooling faster than the nose gives martensite.

heat-treatment-003.question: Adding alloying elements such as Mn, Cr and Mo to steel improves its hardenability. Which is the correct reason?
choices: The nose of the TTT diagram moves to shorter times, so austenite transforms faster
The nose of the TTT diagram moves to longer times, so martensite forms more easily even with slow cooling
The Ms temperature rises, so martensite starts to form earlier in cooling
heat-treatment-003.explanation: Hardenability is the depth to which martensite can be obtained by quenching (how readily the steel hardens). Alloying elements such as Mn, Cr and Mo retard the pearlite and bainite transformations of austenite and move the nose of the TTT and CCT diagrams to longer times. This lowers the critical cooling rate, so martensite forms more easily at the center of thick sections or with slower cooling such as oil quenching. If the nose moved to shorter times, the steel would harden less readily. Most alloying elements actually lower the Ms temperature, so that is not the reason for improved hardenability. Hardenability is evaluated with the Jominy end-quench test.

heat-treatment-004.question: What is the main purpose of tempering a quenched steel?
choices: To make the martensite even harder and raise its wear resistance
To increase retained austenite, stabilizing the microstructure and preventing dimensional change
To restore toughness and reduce internal stresses at the cost of some hardness
heat-treatment-004.explanation: As-quenched martensite is hard but very brittle and carries large internal stresses. In tempering, the steel is reheated to a temperature below the A1 temperature (727 °C); the supersaturated carbon precipitates as fine carbides and internal stresses relax, so hardness falls but toughness recovers substantially. The higher the tempering temperature, the softer and tougher the structure; low-temperature tempering is used for tools and high-temperature tempering for machine parts (the combination with the preceding quench is called quenching and tempering). An increase in hardness on tempering is limited to secondary hardening in certain alloy steels and is not the general purpose. Tempering tends to decompose retained austenite; increasing it is not the aim.

heat-treatment-005.question: The yield stress of a steel follows the Hall–Petch relation σy = σ₀ + k/√d with σ₀ = 70 MPa and k = 0.74 MPa·√m. Which value is closest to the yield stress for an average grain size d = 25 µm?
choices: About 75 MPa
About 148 MPa
About 218 MPa
heat-treatment-005.explanation: Converting the grain size to meters gives d = 25×10⁻⁶ m and √d = 5.0×10⁻³ √m, so k/√d = 0.74/(5.0×10⁻³) = 148 MPa. Hence σy = 70 + 148 = 218 MPa. About 75 MPa results from leaving the grain size in mm as d = 0.025, so the units of k (MPa·√m) and of the grain size do not match. About 148 MPa is only the grain boundary strengthening contribution, forgetting to add σ₀. Grain refinement is one of the few strengthening methods that raises strength and toughness at the same time, and it is exploited in processes such as controlled rolling of steel. When the grain size shrinks to the nanometer scale, the relation can break down.

heat-treatment-006.question: The yield stress of a metal was 150 MPa at an average grain size of 100 µm and 250 MPa at 25 µm. Assuming the Hall–Petch relation σy = σ₀ + k/√d, which value is closest to the yield stress at a grain size of 4 µm?
choices: About 278 MPa
About 550 MPa
About 950 MPa
heat-treatment-006.explanation: Converting the grain sizes to meters and computing 1/√d gives 100 for d = 100 µm, 200 for 25 µm and 500 for 4 µm (all in 1/√m). From the two data points, k = (250 − 150)/(200 − 100) = 1.0 MPa·√m and σ₀ = 150 − 1.0 × 100 = 50 MPa, so at 4 µm, σy = 50 + 1.0 × 500 = 550 MPa. About 950 MPa is the mistake of drawing a straight line assuming the yield stress is proportional to 1/d, and about 278 MPa extrapolates as if the yield stress varied linearly with grain size d. The strengthening is inversely proportional to the square root of the grain size, so each time the grain size is reduced to 1/4, the grain boundary contribution doubles.

heat-treatment-007.question: Which is the correct sequence for precipitation hardening an Al-Cu alloy (duralumin type)?
choices: Solution treatment → quench → aging
Aging → solution treatment → slow cooling
Quench → solution treatment → annealing
heat-treatment-007.explanation: First, a solution treatment holds the alloy above the solvus to dissolve the Cu, and quenching carries the supersaturated solid solution down to room temperature. Holding it at room temperature (natural aging) or at about 100–200 °C (artificial aging) then forms fine precipitates that are coherent or semicoherent with the matrix, such as GP zones, θ″ and θ′, which obstruct dislocation motion and raise the strength. Aging for too long coarsens the stable θ phase (Al₂Cu) and lowers the strength, which is overaging. Slow cooling after solution treatment precipitates coarse equilibrium phases that do not help strengthening, so the quench is essential.

heat-treatment-008.question: Which of the following aluminum alloys cannot be strengthened by precipitation-hardening heat treatment (that is, is non-heat-treatable)?
choices: 2000 series (Al-Cu)
5000 series (Al-Mg)
6000 series (Al-Mg-Si)
heat-treatment-008.explanation: The 5000 series (Al-Mg) are non-heat-treatable alloys that get their strength from solid-solution strengthening by Mg and from work hardening by cold working. They have excellent corrosion resistance and weldability and are used for ships and tanks. The 2000 series (Al-Cu), typified by duralumin, are heat-treatable and strengthened by Al-Cu precipitates. The 6000 series (Al-Mg-Si) are also heat-treatable, using Mg-Si precipitates, and are widely used for extrusions. In addition, the 7000 series (Al-Zn-Mg) are the strongest heat-treatable alloys, while the 1000 series (pure aluminum) and 3000 series (Al-Mn) are non-heat-treatable. Learn to tell from the alloy system whether the strengthening mechanism is precipitation or work hardening.

heat-treatment-009.question: Which statement about substitutional solid-solution strengthening is correct?
choices: The larger the size difference between solute and solvent atoms, the smaller the strengthening effect
Increasing the solute concentration generally lowers strength and raises ductility
The lattice strain field around solute atoms interacts with dislocations and hinders their motion
heat-treatment-009.explanation: Solute atoms differ from the host atoms in size and elastic modulus, so they create lattice strain fields around themselves. These strain fields interact with the strain fields of dislocations and pin them, so a larger stress is needed to move dislocations. This is solid-solution strengthening, and the effect is larger the greater the atomic size difference (size effect) and the modulus difference. Within the solubility limit, increasing the solute concentration generally raises strength and slightly lowers ductility. Brass (Cu-Zn), Al-Mg alloys, and Si and Mn in steel are typical examples of solid-solution strengthening.

heat-treatment-010.question: A copper wire 10.0 mm in diameter is drawn down to 8.0 mm. What is the percent cold work (reduction in area)?
heat-treatment-010.explanation: Percent cold work is the reduction in cross-sectional area, %CW = (A₀ − A_d)/A₀ × 100. Because area is proportional to the square of the diameter, %CW = (10.0² − 8.0²)/10.0² × 100 = (100 − 64)/100 × 100 = 36%. 20% is the reduction in diameter, (10.0 − 8.0)/10.0, and 56% is the mistake of dividing by the area after drawing ((100 − 64)/64 ≈ 0.56). The greater the cold work, the higher the dislocation density and the more the metal work-hardens: strength rises but ductility falls. The amount of cold work also affects the recrystallization temperature and the grain size after recrystallization.

heat-treatment-011.question: Which statement about recrystallization when a cold-worked metal is heated is correct?
choices: New, nearly strain-free grains form; strength falls and ductility is restored
The greater the cold work, the higher the recrystallization temperature
Once recrystallization is complete, the grains do not grow even if heating continues
heat-treatment-011.explanation: When a cold-worked metal is heated, recovery occurs first, as dislocations rearrange and internal stresses fall; at higher temperatures, recrystallization follows, with new, nearly strain-free grains nucleating and growing, driven by the stored strain energy. Because the dislocation density drops greatly, strength and hardness decrease and ductility is restored. The greater the cold work, the larger the stored energy, so the recrystallization temperature is lower. A rough guide for the recrystallization temperature is 0.3–0.5 times the melting point (in absolute temperature), but it varies with the amount of cold work and the purity. If heating continues after recrystallization, grain growth proceeds to reduce the grain boundary energy.

heat-treatment-012.question: An aluminum alloy reaches peak hardness after 10 hours of aging at 190 °C. If the aging rate follows the Arrhenius form with an activation energy of 120 kJ/mol, which value is closest to the time needed to reach peak hardness at 160 °C? Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 1.2 hours
About 12 hours
About 87 hours
heat-treatment-012.explanation: If the reaction rate is proportional to exp(−Q/RT), the time to reach the same state is t ∝ exp(Q/RT). With T₁ = 463 K and T₂ = 433 K, t₂ = t₁ × exp[(Q/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)] = 10 × exp(14433 × 1.495×10⁻⁴) = 10 × exp(2.16) ≈ 87 hours. About 1.2 hours reverses the sign of the exponent, giving a shorter time even though the temperature was lowered. About 12 hours assumes the time is inversely proportional to the temperature in °C. The roughly ninefold increase in time for a difference of only 30 °C reflects the strong temperature dependence of the Arrhenius form.
